# The Agent Pantry — AI Agent Landscape (full)

> 416 AI agent frameworks and tools across 15 categories, scanned from GitHub. Last updated 2026-10-01. Machine-readable JSON: https://theagentpantry.com/data.json

## Agent Frameworks (32)
When to use: Use to build a single agent in code: prompting, tool-calling, the reasoning loop. Pick one as your foundation.
What it is: Libraries for building a single agent in code — they wrap the model call in a loop that can use tools, parse structured output, and decide what to do next.
Problem it addresses: A raw model call just returns text. Turning that into an agent that can call functions, retry, validate output, and chain steps means writing a lot of plumbing (prompt templates, tool schemas, parsing, error handling) that's easy to get wrong.
How it helps: Frameworks give you batteries-included primitives — tool/function calling, structured outputs, the reasoning loop, memory hooks, streaming — so you describe the agent's tools and goal and the library runs the loop.
Technical 101: Most expose an "agent" abstraction over chat completions with tool-calling: you register typed tools, the model emits tool calls, the framework executes them and feeds results back until the model produces a final answer. LangChain and LlamaIndex are broad ecosystems; Pydantic-AI and the OpenAI/Google SDKs emphasize typed, production-grade loops; DSPy compiles prompts as programs you optimize rather than hand-tune.

## Orchestration & Multi-Agent (31)
When to use: Use when one agent isn’t enough and you need several agents, roles, hand-offs, or a workflow/graph.
What it is: Frameworks for coordinating multiple agents (or multiple steps) — assigning roles, passing work between them, and defining the control flow as a graph or workflow.
Problem it addresses: One agent with one prompt struggles with big, multi-stage tasks. Splitting work across specialized agents (planner, researcher, coder, reviewer) needs a way to route messages, share state, and control who runs when — otherwise you get loops, lost context, and chaos.
How it helps: These tools model the team: define agents and their roles, the hand-offs between them, and a graph/state machine that decides execution order, with shared memory and stopping conditions.
Technical 101: Approaches range from conversational (AutoGen's agents that message each other) to role-based crews (CrewAI) to explicit state graphs (LangGraph) where nodes are steps and edges are transitions with checkpointing. The graph model gives you deterministic control, retries, and human-in-the-loop pauses that free-form agent chatter lacks.

## Autonomous Agents (22)
When to use: Use when you want a goal-driven agent that plans and runs long tasks on its own (great as reference designs).
What it is: Goal-driven agents that take a high-level objective and try to plan and execute the whole thing on their own — breaking it into steps, running tools, and iterating until done.
Problem it addresses: Most agents do one bounded task. Some goals ("research X and write a report", "build this app") need open-ended planning, self-correction, and long-running execution that a single prompt can't cover.
How it helps: Autonomous agents add a plan-act-observe-reflect loop on top of a model: they generate a task list, execute tasks with tools, evaluate results, and replan — running for many steps with little supervision.
Technical 101: Pioneered by AutoGPT and BabyAGI, these use the model as a planner that writes and reprioritizes a task queue, plus tools (web, files, code) to act. They're powerful demos but can loop, drift, or burn tokens, so treat most as reference designs and add guardrails — budgets, approvals, sandboxes — before production.

## Coding Agents (33)
When to use: Use when you want an agent that reads, writes, refactors and ships code in your repo or editor.
What it is: Agents specialized for software — they read your repository, write and edit code, run commands and tests, and ship changes, usually inside an editor, terminal, or CI.
Problem it addresses: General chat models can suggest code but can't navigate a real codebase, run the build, see the errors, and iterate. Doing that by hand — copy-pasting between editor and chat — is slow and loses context.
How it helps: Coding agents connect the model to your files, shell, and tests so it can grep the repo, make multi-file edits, run the code, read failures, and fix them — turning "suggest a snippet" into "implement and verify a change".
Technical 101: They combine repo indexing/retrieval, a tool loop (read/write file, run command, search), and a diff/patch format the model emits. SWE-agent and OpenHands target autonomous issue-fixing; Aider, Cline and Continue integrate with your editor/terminal for pair-programming. Quality hinges on test feedback and how well the agent grounds edits in the actual code.

## Skills & Recipes (35)
When to use: Use to give your agent ready-made, reusable skills/recipes instead of hand-writing every behavior.
What it is: Packaged, reusable "skills" — prompt + tools + instructions for a specific capability — and the opinionated harnesses and registries that let an agent load many of them on demand.
Problem it addresses: Re-teaching an agent the same procedure (how to open a PR, run research, format a doc) in every project is wasteful, and giant prompts bloat context. Teams want to share proven agent behaviors like libraries.
How it helps: Skills externalize behavior into small, named units the agent discovers and loads only when relevant, so you compose capabilities instead of hand-writing each one — and version and share them across projects.
Technical 101: A skill is typically a folder with a description, instructions, and optional scripts/tools; the harness indexes them and injects the right one based on the task, keeping context small. Anthropic's Skills define the format; gstack, superpowers and mattpocock/skills are opinionated collections and harnesses for coding agents like Claude Code.

## Browser & Computer Use (22)
When to use: Use when your agent must act in a real browser, GUI, or desktop by seeing the screen and clicking.
What it is: Agents that operate a real browser, GUI, or desktop the way a person does — seeing the screen and clicking, typing, and navigating.
Problem it addresses: Lots of software has no API. To book a flight, fill a portal, or test a web app, an agent must drive the actual interface, which means perceiving a screen and producing mouse/keyboard actions reliably.
How it helps: These tools give the model eyes and hands: they screenshot or read the accessibility tree, let the model decide the next action, and execute clicks and keystrokes — automating any app that has a UI.
Technical 101: Two main approaches: DOM/accessibility-driven (browser-use, Playwright-based) which read structured page elements, and vision-driven (OmniParser, UI-TARS) which parse pixels into clickable regions for screen/OS control. Reliability comes from grounding each action to the right element and recovering when the UI changes.

## Memory & Knowledge (31)
When to use: Use to give your agent long-term memory and retrieval over your own knowledge (RAG, vector stores).
What it is: Systems that give an agent long-term memory and retrieval over your own data — vector stores, memory layers, and RAG pipelines that fetch relevant facts at query time.
Problem it addresses: Models have a fixed context window and no memory between sessions, and they don't know your private or up-to-date data. Stuffing everything into the prompt is impossible and expensive.
How it helps: These store knowledge and past interactions outside the model and retrieve just the relevant pieces to ground each response — so the agent "remembers" users and answers from your documents instead of hallucinating.
Technical 101: RAG embeds your data into vectors, stores them in a database (Qdrant, Weaviate, Chroma), and at query time retrieves the nearest chunks to add to the prompt. Memory layers (mem0, Zep, Letta) add summarization, user/session memory, and knowledge graphs so relevant context persists and is recalled across turns.

Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot, OpenCode + More https://github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem
- mem0ai/mem0 (66k★, HN 201, Python) — The Memory Layer for AI Agents - Drop-in memory infrastructure for AI agents and apps. Context that persists. Built for production. https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0

## Data & Documents (23)
When to use: Use to turn messy docs, PDFs and web pages into clean, structured text your agent or RAG can consume.
What it is: Tools that turn messy, real-world inputs — PDFs, Office docs, HTML, scans — into clean, structured text and chunks an agent or RAG system can actually use.
Problem it addresses: Your knowledge lives in formats models can't read well: complex PDFs, tables, slide decks, images, websites. Feeding raw bytes in produces garbage; you need faithful extraction first.
How it helps: These parse and normalize documents — layout, tables, headings, OCR — into markdown/JSON, and crawl and clean web pages, so the downstream agent gets accurate, well-segmented content.
Technical 101: Converters like markitdown and docling preserve document structure (headings, tables, reading order) and OCR scans; unstructured and loaders split content into typed elements; web tools like Firecrawl and Jina Reader render and strip pages to LLM-friendly markdown. Extraction quality and chunking strategy directly determine RAG accuracy.

Projects:
- microsoft/markitdown (188k★, HN 329, Python) — Python tool for converting files and office documents to Markdown. https://github.com/microsoft/markitdown
- firecrawl/firecrawl (187k★, TypeScript) — 🔥 Supercharge your AI agents with data from the web and beyond. A web data API to search, scrape, and access more sources. https://github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl
- docling-project/docling (68k★, HN 3, Python) — Get your documents ready for gen AI https://github.com/docling-project/docling

## Tools & Protocols (31)
When to use: Use to connect your agent to external tools and to other agents via standards like MCP and A2A.
What it is: Open standards and servers that connect agents to external tools and to each other — most notably the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent-to-agent (A2A) protocols.
Problem it addresses: Every tool integration used to be bespoke glue code, and every framework reinvented it. Without a standard, tools aren't portable across agents and agents can't interoperate.
How it helps: A shared protocol lets any compliant agent discover and call any compliant tool, server, or other agent, so integrations are written once and reused everywhere — like a USB port for AI tools.
Technical 101: MCP defines a client-server spec where servers expose tools, resources, and prompts over a standard transport that any MCP client (Claude, IDEs, frameworks) can use. A2A standardizes agent-to-agent messaging and capability discovery. The payoff is a growing marketplace of reusable servers instead of N×M custom integrations.

Projects:
- modelcontextprotocol/servers (91k★, HN 5, TypeScript) — Model Context Protocol Servers https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers
- ComposioHQ/composio (30k★, HN 7, TypeScript) — Composio powers 1000+ toolkits, tool search, context management, authentication, and a sandboxed workbench to help you build AI agents that turn intent into action. https://github.com/ComposioHQ/composio

## Sandboxes & MicroVMs (30)
When to use: Use when your agent runs untrusted code or tools and you need an isolated, safe place to execute it.
What it is: Isolated execution environments — microVMs and sandboxes — where an agent can run code, install packages, and use a shell without touching your machine or production.
Problem it addresses: Agents that execute model-generated code are a security risk: that code can delete files, exfiltrate secrets, or run forever. You need to run it somewhere disposable and contained, with hard limits.
How it helps: These give each agent run a fresh, locked-down box — filesystem, network, CPU/memory limits, fast startup and teardown — so untrusted code runs safely and reproducibly, then is thrown away.
Technical 101: MicroVMs like Firecracker boot a minimal hardware-virtualized guest in ~100ms — stronger isolation than containers at near-container speed. E2B, microsandbox and agent-sandbox package this as code-interpreter/agent runtimes with SDKs; the tradeoff is isolation strength versus startup latency and resource overhead.

Projects:
- firecracker-microvm/firecracker (37k★, HN 99, Rust) — Secure and fast microVMs for serverless computing. https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker
- trycua/cua (28k★, HN 307, HTML) — Scale computer-use 2.0 with open-source drivers, cross-OS fleets, and benchmarks for training, evaluation, and data generation. https://github.com/trycua/cua
- e2b-dev/E2B (14k★, HN 369, Python) — Open-source, secure environment with real-world tools for enterprise-grade agents. https://github.com/e2b-dev/E2B

## Observability & Eval (13)
When to use: Use to trace, evaluate and monitor what your agent actually did — in development and in production.
What it is: Tooling to see and measure what your agent actually did — tracing each step and LLM call, evaluating output quality, and monitoring cost, latency, and errors in dev and production.
Problem it addresses: Agents are non-deterministic and multi-step, so when they give a wrong or expensive answer it's hard to know which prompt, tool, or step caused it. You can't improve what you can't measure.
How it helps: These capture full traces of prompts, tool calls, and responses, let you score outputs with evals/test sets, and dashboard cost, latency, and failures — so you can debug regressions and prove quality before shipping.
Technical 101: Tracing tools (Langfuse, Phoenix, OpenLLMetry) instrument each LLM/tool span, often via OpenTelemetry, with token and cost accounting. Eval frameworks (DeepEval and others) run datasets through your agent and grade with metrics or LLM-as-judge. Together they form the observe-evaluate-improve loop for non-deterministic systems.

Projects:
- langfuse/langfuse (35k★, HN 215, TypeScript) — 🪢 Open source agent evals & observability: Trace, evaluate, and improve LLM applications with one open platform. https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse
- promptfoo/promptfoo (26k★, HN 5, TypeScript) — Test your prompts, agents, and RAGs. Red teaming/pentesting/vulnerability scanning for AI. Compare performance of GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and more. Simple declarative configs with command line and CI/CD integration. Used by OpenAI and Anthropic. https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo
- comet-ml/opik (22k★, HN 86, Python) — Debug, evaluate, and monitor your LLM applications, RAG systems, and agentic workflows with comprehensive tracing, automated evaluations, and production-ready dashboards. https://github.com/comet-ml/opik

## Runtimes & Platforms (27)
When to use: Use to assemble or host an agent with little-to-no code: low-code builders, workflow automation, hosting.
What it is: Low-code/no-code builders and hosting platforms that let you assemble, deploy, and run agents and workflows with minimal coding — often a visual canvas plus integrations.
Problem it addresses: Not every team wants to write and operate agent code. Building a chatbot or workflow from scratch — wiring models, tools, memory, and a UI, then hosting it — is a lot of undifferentiated work.
How it helps: These provide drag-and-drop flow builders, prebuilt connectors, and managed hosting so non-engineers (and engineers in a hurry) can ship an agent or automation fast.
Technical 101: Platforms like Flowise, Langflow and Dify expose nodes — models, retrievers, tools, logic — on a visual graph that compiles to a runnable app with an API/UI; n8n and Activepieces focus on workflow automation across SaaS. The tradeoff is speed and accessibility versus the flexibility and version control of code.

- n8n-io/n8n (206k★, HN 34, TypeScript) — Fair-code workflow automation platform with native AI capabilities. Combine visual building with custom code, self-host or cloud, 400+ integrations. https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n

## Voice & Speech (30)
When to use: Use when your agent needs to listen (speech-to-text), talk (text-to-speech), or hold a live voice call.
What it is: Models and frameworks for the audio side of agents — speech-to-text (ASR) to hear, text-to-speech (TTS) to speak, and realtime pipelines for live voice conversations.
Problem it addresses: Many use cases — phone support, assistants, accessibility — need spoken interaction, which requires fast, accurate transcription, natural-sounding speech, and low end-to-end latency that's hard to stitch together yourself.
How it helps: ASR models turn audio into text the agent can reason over, TTS turns its replies into speech, and realtime frameworks handle streaming, turn-taking, and interruption so conversations feel natural.
Technical 101: Whisper (and faster-whisper/WhisperX) are the de facto open ASR models; TTS engines like Coqui, Piper and Fish-Speech synthesize voices, some cloning from a sample. Orchestrators like LiveKit Agents and Pipecat wire mic→ASR→LLM→TTS→speaker with barge-in and sub-second latency for live calls.

## Models & Serving (31)
When to use: Use when you want to run or host the LLM yourself — your own hardware or cloud — instead of calling a hosted API.
What it is: The infrastructure that runs the large language models your agent thinks with — engines and servers that load model weights and turn prompts into tokens, plus gateways that route requests across many models.
Problem it addresses: Hosted model APIs are convenient but cost per token, send your data to a third party, and lock you to one vendor's models and rate limits. Many teams need to run open-weight models on their own GPUs for cost, privacy, latency, or offline use.
How it helps: These tools load and serve models efficiently (batching, KV-cache, quantization) so you get high throughput on your own hardware, and gateways give you one OpenAI-compatible endpoint in front of any model so you can swap or load-balance without changing code.
Technical 101: Inference engines like vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp implement paged attention, continuous batching and GGUF/quantized weights to maximize tokens/sec per GPU. Runners like Ollama and LocalAI wrap them in a simple local server; gateways like LiteLLM normalize 100+ providers behind the OpenAI API. Stacks like NVIDIA NeMo and TensorRT-LLM target large-scale, GPU-optimized deployment.

Projects:
- ollama/ollama (182k★, HN 217, Go) — Get up and running with Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, DeepSeek, gpt-oss, Qwen, Gemma and other models. https://github.com/ollama/ollama
- huggingface/transformers (167k★, HN 103, Python) — 🤗 Transformers: the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning models in text, vision, audio, and multimodal models, for both inference and training. https://github.com/huggingface/transformers
- ggml-org/llama.cpp (130k★, HN 839, C++) — LLM inference in C/C++ https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp

## Open Models (25)
When to use: Use to choose the actual open-weight model — DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen, gpt-oss — that your agent reasons with, then run it with a tool from Models & Serving.
What it is: The open-weight large language models themselves — the actual neural-network weights your agent uses to reason — published on Hugging Face. Distinct from the serving tools that run them.
Problem it addresses: Closed APIs (GPT, Claude) are easy but cost per token, can't be self-hosted, and can change under you. To own your stack — for cost, privacy, fine-tuning, or offline use — you need open-weight models you can download and run.
How it helps: Open models give you weights you can host anywhere, fine-tune on your own data, and swap freely. Hugging Face is the hub where they're published, versioned, and compared by downloads and community likes, so you can pick the right size and license.
Technical 101: Models ship as weight files (safetensors) plus a config, tagged by task (text-generation), size, and license. Families like DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen, Mistral and gpt-oss trade size against quality; quantized GGUF variants shrink them to run on modest hardware. Pair a model here with an engine from Models & Serving (vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama) to actually run it.

Projects:
- openai/gpt-oss-120b (5.3k★, text-generation) — Open-weight text-generation on Hugging Face · transformers. https://huggingface.co/openai/gpt-oss-120b
